content: There are numerous pathological conditions that can result in elevated levels of unconjugated bilirubin (hyperbilirubinaemia) in neonates. The current standard treatments for this condition include phototherapy and, in more severe cases, exchange transfusion. In addition to phototherapy, clofibrate has been investigated as a potential treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia in various countries. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of clofibrate when used in combination with phototherapy, compared to phototherapy alone, in the treatment of unconjugated neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia. Randomised controlled trials were identified through systematic searches of databases including MEDLINE (1950 to April 2012), The Cochrane Library, EMBASE (1980 to April 2012), and CINAHL. The final search was conducted on April 2, 2012. Trials were included if they involved neonates with hyperbilirubinaemia who received either clofibrate combined with phototherapy, phototherapy alone, or placebo combined with phototherapy. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers. The outcomes assessed included the mean change in bilirubin levels, the mean duration of phototherapy, the number of exchange transfusions required, adverse effects of clofibrate, the incidence of bilirubin encephalopathy, and neonatal mortality. Study authors were contacted for additional information, and the methodological quality of the studies was assessed using a Risk of bias table. Fifteen studies were included in the review, with two involving preterm neonates and 13 involving term neonates. All but one of these studies were conducted in Iran. For preterm neonates, the group receiving 100 mg/kg of clofibrate demonstrated significantly lower bilirubin levels compared to the control group, with a mean difference of ‐1.37 mg/dL (95% CI ‐2.19 mg/dL to ‐0.55 mg/dL) (‐23 µmol/L; 95% CI ‐36 µmol/L to ‐9 µmol/L) after 48 hours of treatment. Among term neonates, bilirubin levels were also significantly lower in the clofibrate group compared to the control group after both 24 and 48 hours of treatment. The weighted mean differences were ‐2.14 mg/dL (95% CI ‐2.53 mg/dL to ‐1.75 mg/dL) (‐37 µmol/L; 95% CI ‐43 µmol/L to ‐30 µmol/L) and ‐1.82 mg/dL (95% CI ‐2.25 mg/dL to ‐1.38 mg/dL) (‐31 µmol/L; 95% CI ‐38 µmol/L to ‐24 µmol/L), respectively. The duration of phototherapy was significantly shorter in the clofibrate group compared to the control group for both preterm and term neonates. The weighted mean differences were ‐23.82 hours (95% CI ‐30.46 hours to ‐17.18 hours) for preterm neonates and ‐25.40 hours (95% CI ‐28.94 hours to ‐21.86 hours) for term neonates. None of the included studies reported on the rates of bilirubin encephalopathy, neonatal mortality, or the levels of parental or staff satisfaction with the interventions. The authors concluded that there is insufficient data from multiple countries to make definitive recommendations regarding the use of clofibrate in combination with phototherapy for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia. Furthermore, clofibrate has been withdrawn from the market in some countries due to safety concerns and is no longer used in adults for its primary indication. Consequently, this review will no longer be updated.
